segments.text: Thank you

I do want to clarify one thing before you start posting on social media that Microsoft is in the house. I am not here as an official Microsoft representative. I am here because of my 16 plus years in nuclear prior to switching to tech.

I worked at a nuclear plant in Michigan. This is all US-based for six years, right after university. Then I worked for the Vogel Project in Georgia for 10 years in construction, commissioning and testing, in engineering, and also the turnover from commissioning and testing to operations.

So yes, I am a director at Microsoft, but I am here because of my passion for nuclear. And as a daughter of the African continent, I felt the duty to support this great vision. And that's why we're here.

This brings us to our panel session today, which is really building off of what the sessions from yesterday. Yesterday, we learned a few things. Number one, there will be a nuclear power plant in Rwanda in the next decade.
The decision has been made. There's no questions asked. We're just moving forward.

Number two, we learned yesterday that the financing of this project, what I gathered is money is not the problem. It's the structure of the deal. To make sure that our lenders are confident that we will pay back, and that also that we understand the special and unique technology that nuclear is, and that it's all embedded in the structure.

With that in mind, knowing that we will have a nuclear plant in Rwanda, and it will be financed, what we're going to talk about now is, are our industries ready? How are we going to support? This is what this session is about. And I'm going to start off with a question to all the panelists, really wanting to know, how can industrial demand support nuclear project bankability? And I will start with the Honorable Minister, Paula Ngabire. Thank you very much.

Good morning, everyone. And for our first time guests, welcome to Kigali. We hope it's going to be the first of many visits as you come back to do business with us, to invest in Rwanda, and to really contribute to the development of our country.

But coming back to your question, I think it's very much wrapped in the context that you said at the beginning, which is really, it's not about the money. It's really understanding where the demand is, and how do we catalyze that demand so that the right investments can be made in nuclear energy? When you look globally, and I think this is not unique to Africa itself, you realize that traditional nuclear projects suffer from high upfront capex and long payback periods. And what that means is that if you're going to be sourcing financing for this kind of project, then you have to make sure that they are bankable.

And the bankability logic is very straightforward. It's straightforward in the sense that if you have a nuclear project that demonstrates about 60 to 70% of the output is anchored around an industrial off-taker, then that project looks different from if you're hoping that this is just going to be connected to the grid, and hopefully we can find the demand for that. And so as we think about industrial off-takers, whether it's the mines, the smelters, data centers, what lenders are looking for is predictability.

As you rightly say, they're looking for 24-7 credit-worthy best load demand. And the natural anchors for that are going to be sectors where you know that a simple power outage is going to cost billions of dollars in revenues lost because of that outage. And so the natural anchors are going to be data centers, going to be advanced manufacturing, going to look at mineral processing.

And that's why even for Rwanda, as we announced that in the next decade, maybe seven years, we should be able to have an SMR, we have already started with understanding what is going to be the off-takers, thinking about those off-takers as a government and making sure that those are going to be ready when these facilities up and running so that we can render it bankable, we can render it useful, but it can also contribute to the development of our country. And I'll end on this. When you think about the energy architecture that is required, especially for nations that are trying to compete in a world where AI workloads, mineral processing, are primary determinants for industrial competitiveness, then the conversation around energy becomes a priority for everyone.

It's not an afterthought, it's not a parallel investment, but rather things that you do sequentially to ensure that you have the right environment for those industries to grow and contribute competitively, but also to make sure that you're not looking at anything that could hinder development in any form. These great insights, really great insights. We do wanna hear from you, Mr. Sene.

From your perspective, how do you think industrial demand supports nuclear bankability? Thanks and good morning, everyone. So let me first start by maybe talking about the demand, which is more related to us as human beings. So I'll be talking more about food, which is the area where we are.

And when we talk about food, we talk about the food system. And within that system, you also have industries and packaging and processing. So today, I think we are 1.5 billion on the continent and also the world, 7 billion, 9 billion coming.
So the renewable energy we have on a daily basis is food before we come here, so otherwise you can't function. So it's a demand on a daily basis. You cannot postpone it.

The fact that it is a demand, demand also for us to get that food reliable, constant, but also nutritious and available on time. So now when you look at the agri-food system value chain, from research to production, processing, transport, to export, along that food system value chain, you have a higher demand on energy. So for so long, we have been always innovating in the agri-food system value chain with renewable energy.
We have sun in Africa. You have geothermal, you have wind, but we have never talked about nuclear, which is also renewable. So I've never seen it before.

Even in the literature myself, I've been a climate finance expert in the past, designing and structuring projects on energy, nexus agriculture, but bringing now nuclear as part of it, will be a game changer. First, because today, as the way we structure our production to be competitive, because again, 100 billion of import in Africa, we export jobs, and we are not adding value on our raw material. It is being exported, transformed, and we sell again to Africa, more expensive.
So the leadership is, we have to shift this. To shift it, you need industrialization. That industrialization also to bring young people.
We have 70% of our population young. They won't come into agriculture if it is not attractive or how we call it, sexy. So attractivity means energy, and energy means modernization.

It also means competitiveness. And to get there, aggregation will be extremely important in some production poles or agropoles, agroparks. And once we have that one, so you can plug in the energy source and then make it also bankable, the predictability will be there, the credit worthiness and scale.

And it's very important to bring it along the food system, value chain, which will help us also move forward when it comes to industrialization of the continent, but also feeding the continent and creating jobs for our young people. great perspective on the agriculture side of things. Now we're gonna move to the workforce side of things.

So Dr. Aristide, in your perspective, when you think about what you do, how can industrial demand support nuclear project bankability? Thank you, Magali, for asking that question. Hello everyone. In fact, the question I've been asking myself since the advent of artificial intelligence, the demand for data centers has increased by 10 to 100 times.

Today, large data centers consume the equivalent of a city of 200,000 inhabitants, more or less. So in an African context where several countries still have problems with unloading or sometimes you have to stop industries to be able to make it work, to be able to feed the households. How do we install data centers so that they can work in a tense energy context? So the question I ask myself, especially since it's about what economic models can be put in place to finance nuclear energy, is what do we do? Do we have to install data centers in this context or do we invest in SMRs to be able to have data centers? And when we say that we invest in SMRs, it means that someone has to put that money there.
How are we going to do it? This is the question that is open and that I open here and that we can detail later. Thank you. Thank you.

Okay, now we get to the diplomacy side of life. We have our UN representative here, Mr. Amandeep Singh Gill. In your perspective, based on the work that you do, how do you think industrial demand supports nuclear project bankability? Thank you very much, Magali.

Like you, I have a nuclear pass, which is perhaps why I'm here in addition to the current focus on artificial intelligence and digital and emerging technologies. And I've had the privilege of visiting the site when it was under construction. Now, we can look at this issue from the perspective of demand and bankability, which is the most important lesson coming out of this conference.

I think the key issue is not the availability of technology or sites. They are there. The key issue is how do we structure the offtake? So the credit structure behind the demand and how that's turned into long-term power purchase agreements that make nuclear energy a financeable infrastructure, long-term infrastructure.

And I'll pick just one area to illustrate this. So all of Africa has just 1% of the world's data center capacity. And you have the five leading data markets in Africa, South Africa, Kenya, Morocco, Egypt, Nigeria.

And anchored in those markets, you obviously have a great demand for the data and AI-related infrastructure. And if you look at the global perspective, you have today the hyperscalers, the leading tech companies that have 45 gigawatts of conditional commitments with SMRs in terms of offtake. And they are often able to provide guarantees that are even better than sovereigns.

So the key question from my perspective is how do we bring these two aspects together? Obviously, there are other areas of demand, you know, mining, manufacturing, and you have live examples, for example, from Ghana, in terms of Ghana's recent agreement with Regnum on an SPV centered around industrial offtake. But for me, the key area is data center capacity, AI compute capacity. And if somehow the nuclear energy sector and the data infrastructure can be brought together regionally, hopefully, because that allows you to aggregate more demand, and you can bring the hyperscalers to the equation.

So I think that would allow us to have those 25 to 40-year long-term PPAs that then make this bankable. Like it, love it. All right, we're going to move to our very own CEO of the Rwanda Mines, Petroleum and Gas Board, Alice Uwase

And so we just want to hear from the mining and petroleum and gas perspective. Do you think, in your opinion, like how we can meet that demand to support nuclear project bankability? Thank you very much. Morning.
I know it's still early in the morning, but we need some energy from you also, from the audience. Yes. Interestingly, mining and nuclear industries are interlinked.

Of course, nuclear power plants are powered with minerals, and everything about construction of nuclear power plants is: you need burial metals, you need tungsten, you need all types of minerals. But on the other end, the mineral sector depends heavily on nuclear, the reliable energy from nuclear power plants. So on the manufacturing, let me start from the whole value chain.

The whole mineral value chain depends on a consistent, reliable energy supply from the mine site to be able to mechanize. That means the demand is already there. Currently in Rwanda, we are mechanizing all our mines, but we need a consistent supply of energy to be able to mechanize all the mine sites in the country and have a direct impact on the production, which means it's strategic for us on the other side of the mining sector.

When you transition to value addition, there are some refineries and smelters currently on hold because we don't have the right energy, enough energy in the country. Let's take, for instance, one mineral that is currently in high demand, we call Wolfram, that is the tungsten very in need for, in the defense industry, for drill bits, for the manufacturing industry. We have it here in Rwanda.

And what we've started to negotiate with off-tech agreements to be able to not lose the value addition strategy is to make sure that in the agreement, we say once we have the energy available in Rwanda and we are targeting actually the SMR in the early 2030s, saying once the energy is available, we have together, we have to implement and establish a value addition facility for tungsten because it's not an excuse right now, off-tech agreements, yes, but in the long run, we are planning ahead to make sure that we don't lose the value addition hub. So there is a demand on the mining side and we can, the advantage of SMR is the flexibility in scaling up. So if we take one mineral, there are different steps of refinery, of refining it, meaning in semi-refined metal needs a certain amount of energy.

And if you want to go further, it needs another amount of energy. So there is an opportunity to sequence SMR planning with mineral processing and value addition strategy in the long run and start incorporating them in the agreements and the investment on the ground currently happening in Rwanda. Thank you.
Thank you. So what we've heard so far, and you guys keep me honest, is that there is a demand. From our leaders over here, we just heard on the industrial side, there is a demand.

And I jotted down a few things. There is a need for industrialization and this need for industrialization also requires energy. We heard that mining is closely linked to nuclear, right? And so clearly everybody agrees this is something that needs to be done.

Now in the aggregate, obviously, we need this. Now we're gonna go a little bit more deeper into the various different sections. And I will start with, these are more tailored questions to the various panelists.

And I will start with Honorable Paula Ingabire , our Minister of ICT and Innovation. So the question we have for you is how can Rwanda's growing digital infrastructure, that includes data centers, it includes AI, it includes services. So how is Rwanda needed to support this project? And really across Africa as well, as opposed to just Rwanda, let's think of Rwanda and also across Africa.

So I would even add, I think beyond data centers, cloud infrastructure, AI workloads, I think what we've seen historically is even when you think about the telecommunication landscape is that towers have been one of the major consumers of electricity in the national grid. And what we see is that the electricity costs account for 30 to 50% of the operating costs for towers. So more broadly, as you think about the ICT sector, I think it has a potential of being a demand driver when it comes to clean energy.

But if we zero down to Sub-Saharan Africa, I think what we've seen, and we talked about it in the earlier set of questions is that many of the Sub-Saharan African countries fail to attract nuclear capital, primarily because the consumer electricity demand is very unpredictable and fragmented. So this is where the ICT sector then comes in because it sort of shifts or changes the paradigm by introducing massive centralized demand. And you think about data centers, as you're saying, you're looking for data centers, you need 99.999% uptime.

And so what that means is that you need uptime flatline demand. And usually we'll talk about redundancy and all of those three different lines because that is what is required to keep the services going. Now, when you look at the IAEA report, they talk about global data center power consumption.

Today, that stands at about 415 terawatts per hour. And I think it's growing, we're seeing a 50% annual surge for that. AI particularly, its main constraint globally, not just for Africa, has always been, the primary constraint is always around reliable energy availability.

And just to give context, when you do a simple Google search, you're probably going to use 0.03 watts hours for each single search. When you do a chart GPT query, any general AI query, you're looking at three watts. So basically 10 times the capacity.

And therein lies the rational or justification why technology, the ICT sector in general, can be a long time driver for this electricity demand and become a great anchor for some of these nuclear investments that different countries are making. So let's talk about Rwanda, particularly for Rwanda. One, our data center industry is growing, 35%

We're looking at attracting different hyperscalers. Our ambition is to look at how we can invest in a 100 megawatt data center going forward. And if you think about that in simple terms, well, it's a $5 billion investment, but one where it's least guaranteed that you can find at least $220 million of revenue every year.

And so the numbers speak for themselves. And I think the conversation that we're having here on this panel is then how do we make a case for these kinds of investments to be made by providing these offtakers as we go forward? And I'll give you a simple, and going back to the conversation of bankability, I'll give you a simple example. We're talking about ambitions of having a 100 megawatt data center.

But if you start even with a five megawatt data center, what you'll see is that over a year, you're going to consume at least 45 million worth of kilowatts of power for just a five megawatt data center. And that is already 30 plus million dollar revenues. What we do as we size up and scope the demand is then to make sure that you don't have a single point of failure where it's just one demand driver, but you're really looking at a number of hyperscalers that can come on board.

All of these hyperscalers, Amazon, Google, Nemit, all of them are looking for clean energy. It's part of the metrics. And so if you're able to have a nuclear power plant as SMR that is able to give them this level of credibility and off-tech demand, I think that creates a good justification.

And that is why for Rwanda, as I said earlier, as we're thinking about the SMR, we're already looking at what's going to be our potential demand drivers. We've invested, we're investing in AI use cases in agriculture, healthcare, education, financial services, because we want to create that demand as we build the infrastructure that will support that. I'll end on this.

As a country, we have many ambitions. The first ambition being around the net zero commitments that we already have from an environmental and climate perspective. We definitely have big ambitions around having an accelerated digital economy, and that's seen in proof of the investments that we're making in the digital landscape.

We have an emerging industrial base, and these really have been what is feeding into some of the announcements that we made yesterday in making sure that we already have the demand earmarked and ready once the generation of this power is ready. I love it. I love this idea of de-risking things so that it's ideal for the hyperscaler when they're coming.
Yeah, awesome. All right, let's get to the agriculture side of life. And this is for Mr. Senee.

How can large-scale agro-processing and food value chains help create the long-term electricity demand needed to support nuclear investments, especially through SMRs and MMRs? No, thanks. I think it's a very important question, particularly when you are looking at productive areas in each country. And I will start with maybe two levels.

Number one is at a country level, and number two is at a cross-border, because we also have corridors between different countries. And this is linked to ecosystems, an ecosystem where you know that we can make a difference in terms of specialization of countries when it comes to agro-commodities production, whether it is for local consumption or for export. So on the continent, we have many commodities which we are good at, rice, cocoa, coffee, tea, vegetables, maize, et cetera.

So most of those commodities, the demand is high at the local level, but also demand is high at international level. Now, when we structure agro-production areas, and the way you plan it, number one, we already have these kinds of generators, just in case there is no electricity. So it's already there.

So the network, the grid, they bring it or off-grid, but there is already the conceptual thinking of adding it from first. But most of these ones are fragmented along the food system value chain. So you have the research area where they are doing laboratories, vaccine, and all of this one, when it comes also to livestock, et cetera, they do have also the plug-in of their own energy there and are struggling with.

And later on, you go somewhere very far, you have a production area where it's irrigation systems. And by the way, agriculture in Africa is rain-fed. We are not producing like the 12 months because of this reality.
And that's also linked to climate change. When you change, you have problems. So to be able to produce the entire year, you need energy.
So the demand is there. So why? Because you need to get the water and the water, groundwater, surface water is available. So we also have the numbers on the continent.

So abundant. Now, being able to get that one, you need something like the energy water nexus. And that energy water nexus has to be structured in areas where you have these rivers and those rivers or surface water that is available, structuring the entire agro-industrial pole and agro-zones or agro-poles, however you call it, will require to bring the research center there.

You also aggregate the production there, the logistics and the storage, the greenhouses. So the processing, most of those should be in one area. The moment you start aggregating all these elements of production, which will bring you the final product, which is food.
Today, I think in the continent, we are all very sophisticated. Going in malls to buy, you look at the product, et cetera. And that means you need high energy to be able to get that final product.

That reality makes the situation more predictable, but also bankability. So as a financiers and investors, it's the first de-risking, the structuring and the planning. And those programs are already on the continent.

You have the special program of the African Development Bank, the agro-poles. You have it in many countries. So as we structure those one now, mainstreaming the reality of these nuclear into all those programs, these development institutions, the government guarantee funds, the equity funds, the blended finance became much more easier.
And I'll end with the second level, which is corridors. So we have many corridors, Lopito corridors, West Africa corridors. So those corridors, they follow different countries.

And as part of the Africa Free Trade Agreement and also supporting intra-trade production, productivity and competitiveness, we can also join force between different countries to create those energy infrastructure combined into those different corridors that goes beyond one country and gonna help us also meet the demand in terms of food demand, but at the same time, attract investment. And from an investment perspective and bankability, people are more comfortable now to come in because there is scale and these are large agro-industrial parks, like agro-poles where everything is in. It's just to come and plug in the micro modular reactors or small modular reactors and start powering the entire food system value chain.
Mr. Seneee, your passion for your industry is real. I can see that you're very passionate about agro-processing and you need energy. You definitely need energy.

Thank you. We are going to turn over to Dr. Aristide Boyam, the CEO of DevChampio. So Dr. Aristide, considering DevChampio's track record of identifying and training a thousand plus developers across 20 plus African countries, what specific actions could be taken in the next few years to build a nuclear-ready digital workforce capable of supporting SMR deployment? Thank you, Magali.

In fact, integrating the question of technological skills is really crucial. It's really something important because all this transformation requires skills to support this development. In fact, at DevChampio since 2019, we have created a platform and the goal of this platform is to detect talents in computer programming, cybersecurity and now in artificial intelligence.
So this platform is online. We organize online competitions to detect talents, sometimes that can be outside universities, outside companies. We are going to detect them.

What we do next is to strengthen their skills and we certify them with partners, notably a French partner called Isograde and an Indian partner called Coach Chef. And the idea of having these skills is to make them available to companies or the public sector. So it's to meet that demand.

But Magali, the question we ask ourselves is that all these skills are used in computer development. And we conducted a survey on the platform. More than 80% of developers use artificial intelligence today to develop mobile applications, to develop software.

What does that mean? It means that they will work on platforms that are outside the continent, mainly in America. And so, what are they going to do? It means that the intellectual performance that is made on the continent. I take the case of 1,000 developers.

They will develop solutions every day. And these solutions are generated by platforms that are hosted on data centers that are outside the continent. So what does that mean? It means that the intellectual propositions leave.
So the added value, it's gone. Because as soon as it arrives on the platform, it stays. So that's a real question.

So this question means that with data centers that are outside the continent, all our intellectual position remains outside. And so that's a real question. So for that, of course, we need to integrate data centers in Africa.

And for that, we need energy. And so the idea here is to be able to train young people in data center management issues, but also in SMR. And what does that mean? It means that today, the new technologies that have allowed the development of SMR are more and more digitized.
More and more digitized. It has nothing to do with nuclear power plants from 50 or 60 years ago. Today, it's more and more digitized.

And if it's more and more digitized, it's more and more fragile, in the sense that these power plants can suffer cyber attacks. So, in terms of strategic competence, we need to be able to train young people in cybersecurity issues, in critical industrial systems. So we need to be able to do that.

We also have issues like the engineering of digital twins. What is a digital twin? It's when we model and simulate the operation of a nuclear power plant in order to understand how it works. It's very important.

And we also have issues like predictive maintenance thanks to artificial intelligence. And during our exchanges, I explained to you that I talked to an African entrepreneur who has a solution that actually allows us to rely on hundreds and thousands of data in order to predict and anticipate the incidents that will occur, notably the change of parts, and so on and so forth. So all these skills are skills that we need.

So the idea is very simple. It's to rely on the knowledge that we have from computer engineers, technicians, the talents that we have detected, to add a layer through a training of 6 to 18 months, for example, to be able to have cybersecurity specialists in critical systems, to be able to have engineers capable of developing digital twins, to have engineers capable of doing predictive maintenance, for example, or to use predictive artificial intelligence for documentation. Because we know that in the nuclear sector, there is a lot of technical documentation and it is something very tedious.

And we saw that, we also talked about it before this panel, that the time it took to develop all these systems before has nothing to do with it anymore. And to try a parallel, it was a bit about mining issues. It's that before, even now, when we extract materials in Africa, we have to transform them elsewhere because we have an energy problem.
So we have the problem of artificial intelligence. It's the same thing. It means that we are going to produce texas here to supply it abroad because we don't have the energy.

So this question is crucial. So to sum up, the idea is to say, instead of going back to zero, we have a lot of talent, who are good engineers, who are developing solutions today, applications that are adapted to our context. The idea is to add a layer that corresponds to the needs of the nuclear sector.

So that's what can be done. And for that, the idea is to have partnerships with states or with nuclear operators, nuclear councils. So it will allow us very quickly, I think in the next two or three years, DEV Champion can have collaborations with companies that are already there to be able to provide engineering competence cohorts on digital twins, predictive maintenance or critical cybersecurity.
Thank you. Thank you. I have a follow-up question, and I will say it in French too.
You talked about the young people getting training. What about the older generation? I am now talking about a few older people. Do we think of them too? Of course.

In fact, it is true that we talk more about young people because there has been a real boom in recent years with a lot of technology. But we need the old ones. In fact, what do the old ones bring us? They bring us experience.

And we need that experience. And in fact, the idea is that these old people are a bit like the mentors of the young. Because we realized that, especially all young engineers who learn computer science with artificial intelligence, they lack a small part anyway.
And these seniors, that's what they bring them. In a project, we always need these seniors. It is they who today are able to say, go see in such and such a place what the young people do not see.
So we really need these seniors and they are integrated in the projects. Thank you.
We don't want to forget about another group as well. Thank you. All right.

My next question is to Mr. Amandeep Singh Gill. Thinking about how global technology governance, the frameworks, how can those support the integration of nuclear energy into Africa's growing digital and industrial ecosystems? And particularly for energy-intensive sectors like data centers and advanced manufacturing. What are your thoughts? Thank you, Magali.

So in the last two years, there's been really a paradigm shift in terms of how we look at AI and emerging technologies at the United Nations. So member states have agreed on a new governance framework. Part of it is regular scientific assessments through an independent international scientific panel co-chaired by Yoshua Bengio and Maria Ressa, with seven African AI scientists as well.

Part of it is a regular global dialogue on AI governance. First one in July in Geneva, and next one in May in New York. So all 193 countries have a seat at the table to set the rules of the road for this very powerful technology.

And the third element, which is more relevant for our discussion today, is how do we address the AI divide? And the divide is real. I mentioned just 1% of the data center capacity in Africa. If you look at the computer infrastructure, nearly 80% in US and China, a bit in Europe, and for 5 billion people, just 5% of the total infrastructure.
And this is not only infrastructure, it's talent. Talent is highly concentrated in a few zip codes. It's about data sets.
It's about open and shareable models. So that's a very urgent issue. And I really want to speak to the policymakers in the room.
You know, there's not a moment to waste. There's not a dollar to waste. And the energy aspect is critical.

We already have a lot of energy poverty and food security, you know, other industrialization. The legacy gaps of the past cannot be addressed without reliable electricity. But this piece, AI, is moving so fast, it's going to be so brutally transformative of how we run industries, how we deliver economic value.

There's no moment to lose. I mean, if you look at two recent examples in Africa, the Olkaria project, 1 billion project, Microsoft, G42, Kenya. So that project has to be postponed because the grid is not stable enough to take that load.

You know, even though you're getting it from geothermal energy. If you look at Mozal in Mozambique, the smelter issue, you know, there again, because of drought, the dam is not able to deliver that power. And so the smelter is not operating at full capacity.

Now, this means that you need to up the volume, you need to up the quality, and you need to increase the viability and the reliability of grids. So massive investments are going to be required for which you need to plug into this new source of demand to unlock those long-term PPAs. And, and this is very important, you need to come together regionally because when the hyperscalers are looking at investments, you know, they'll say, okay, makes sense for me to go to Lagos, Cape Town, you know, Casablanca, Nairobi, but you know, what about the rest? So I think sub-regionally, you need to come together, work on grid connectivity, and you need to take a fleet approach to SMR.

So I'm putting on my old nuclear hat, I think talent development, the factory model approach to SMRs, you know, it cannot work unless you have four, five situated in a region, and the region works together to develop the talent, to have sovereignty over some of the engineering choices, because at the end of the day, you know, sovereignty today means AI sovereignty, and AI sovereignty cannot be there without energy sovereignty. So, you know, instead of taking technology from here and there, which may happen, I think to build the common talent pool, to build the common grid management practices, the interoperability, which will also give scale to the African entrepreneurs, you know, if you're connecting the energy infrastructure, if you're connecting the digital public infrastructure, then an African entrepreneur, an AI entrepreneur sitting in Kigali can address the entire continent as, you know, TAM, as total addressable market. So I think those are the critical choices before policymakers here, and there is, as Paola was saying, there is the decarbonization imperative, which for us at the UN is very, very important.

The ICT industry needs decarbonization. You have the C-BAM arrangement coming up in the European Union. So from the start, if the green transition and the AI transition can be brought together, today you have half a million cell phone towers in Africa, and they are burning diesel, and costs are going up, and, you know, just Vodacom Africa is spending hundreds of millions of dollars on energy costs.

So I think this has to be the integrated strategic thinking around AI, around energy, around digital infrastructure. The sub-regional, regional cooperation is so critical. There's not a moment to waste.

I'll end with something a minister told me last year. He said, USG , it's clear to me, AI equals computer equals energy, and energy equals nuclear. So for this minister, finally, the penny had dropped, you know, that this equation is almost brutally linear.
And I think that's what I want the policymakers in this room to take away today. Thanks. Thank you, thank you, sir.

All right, the next question is for Alice Wase. With the growing energy demand from the mining and petroleum sectors, how can Rwanda align industrial expansion with nuclear energy development to attract long-term investment?
